Taking advantage of the fast curing kinetics and the lack of sensitivity to oxygen inhibition, thiol–norbornene silicone composites filled with both light-scattering fillers (fumed nanosilica) and multifunctional additives [graphene oxide (GO)] were investigated for application in 3D printing, microfabrication, and functional conductive silicone coatings. In this study, we introduced a thiol–ene silicone system based on norbornene-terminated and highly functionalized thiol PDMS, which displayed an ultrafast curing speed and excellent tolerance to inhibition by oxygen, which has been a major issue for radical reactions, even with thiol–ene chemistry (_e.g._, incomplete surface cure). Considering the extremely high cure rate coupled with the excellent oxygen inhibition, the ability of the current thiol–norbornene silicone to systematically tailor the formulations for different operating conditions and final network properties are, therefore, highly desirable and strongly attractive for versatile applications in many demanding industry sectors such as AM, microfabrication, and fast coating of functional materials. The thiol-ene polymerization is a step-growth reaction in which a monomer containing multiple sulfhydryl functional groups ("thiols") react with a second monomer featuring multiple vinyl functional groups ("ene") to form a cross-linked polymer. In the work presented by Bowman's group [215], thiol-ene polymerization was demonstrated to be an effective method for step and flash imprint lithography thanks to rapid polymerization rates, minimal oxygen inhibition, near-complete polymerization and lower shrinkage compared to the acrylate polymerization. The greatest advantage of thiol-ene polymers is their potential to provide easy access to surface functionalization, by making use of different stoichiometric ratios of the two monomers during polymerization to produce excess sulfhydryl or allyl functional groups, respectively, on the surfaces of the channels [23,24]. It is con-cluded that, in particular, the rapid prototyping possibility combined with the material’s resulting mechanical strength, solvent resistance, and biocompatibility, as well as the inherently easy surface functionalization, are strong factors to make thiol-ene polymers strong contenders for promising future materials for many biological, clinical and technical lab-on-a-chip applications.
